1:
Ellicott objects to the printers: it is greatly to be regretted, he says, that this verse was prefixed to this chapter, since the section it belongs to is the one before, not the one after — the second verse begins a new series of visions and the first closes the old. He then takes up the harder question the verse raises, whether the sealed roll is ever actually unrolled at all. Some hold that a portion is displayed as each seal is broken; others that the visions merely accompany the openings and are quite distinct from the writing, so that the roll is never read, the last seal producing only a silence. He finds that singularly harsh and argues from the narrative itself: the book of God's purposes was seen in the hand of him on the throne, the seer longed to know its contents, vain efforts were made to open it, he wept with disappointment, and he was comforted by hearing that the Lion of the tribe of Judah had prevailed to open it — and then, on this reading, not a line of it is ever revealed. John gives no hint of so disappointing a conclusion. Only a spirit in bondage to foolish literalisms, he adds, will ask how visions can be the writing in a roll.

What the silence is gets four answers. Clarke calls it a metaphor for deep and solemn expectation, on the ordinary observation that when something prodigious is looked for all is silence and the breath is scarcely heard to be drawn; then he grounds it in the temple, arguing that the chapter alludes strongly to the temple service and so presumes the temple still standing, since while the priest burned incense the people continued in silent prayer outside — which is why the angel who follows appears to execute a priest's office. Wesley makes the point by contrast: such a silence is mentioned in this one place only, and it is remarkable because praise sounds in heaven day and night, and because immediately before it the angels and the innumerable multitude had been crying with a loud voice, so that all is still at once and there is an universal pause. He will not let it stand as the thing itself — silence is only a preparation, and the grand point is the sounding of the trumpets. Henry offers two readings and does not choose: a silence of peace, no complaints going up because all was quiet in the church, or a silence of expectation, as when all flesh is bidden be silent before the Lord.

Robertson describes the effect rather than the cause, following Swete: no elder or angel speaking, no chorus of praise, no thunder from the throne, but a temporary cessation in the revelations; and the word for the half hour is late, rare, and found here alone. Victorinus gives a reason none of the others give, and it is a literary one. The silence signifies the beginning of everlasting rest, but is described as partial and interrupted precisely so that the narrative can go on — for if the silence had continued, here would be the end of the book. Bede reads it as a real interval after the death of Antichrist, taking the extra forty-five days of Daniel's reckoning as Jerome interpreted them, and granting that why there should be silence for those days is a matter of divine knowledge, unless the deferring of the kingdom of the saints is the trial of patience. He then supplies the typology the sequence invites: at the sixth seal the greatest afflictions of the Church, at the seventh rest, since the Lord was crucified on the sixth day of the week and rested on the Sabbath awaiting the resurrection. And he warns that what follows is a recapitulation, the same things about to be said in another manner.
2:
Gill works through the candidates by elimination: not the seven spirits of God, whose names and office differ; not the ministers of the word, though this book often calls them angels; but angelic spirits — and either evil ones, since they execute wrath and bring judgements on the earth, or rather good angels, who are sometimes ministers of wrath themselves. He thinks seven a proper number for seven trumpets and hears behind it the seven princes an eastern monarch kept continually about him. The definite article is the difficulty, since the seven angels reads as though they had been mentioned before. Robertson takes it at face value, that it points to seven well-known figures, and supplies the names Enoch gives to the seven archangels, adding that the idea of angels of the Presence has an Old Testament root, while confessing that we do not know precisely what John had in mind. Barnes argues the opposite, that the article need not imply prior mention, since one may speak of the seven members of a cabinet or the governors of the states without having introduced them, or say he saw an army, and the commander-in-chief, and the four staff officers, and the bands of music. He allows only that standing before God suggests a permanent station, as Gabriel says he stands in the presence of God.

Ellicott uses the verse to set out the architecture of what follows. The trumpet visions run to the end of the eleventh chapter and are arranged in marked correspondence with the visions of the seals: in each series two subordinate visions are interposed towards the end — there the sealed multitude, here the little book and the seven thunders and the measuring of the temple — and their purpose in both cases is the same, to give an insight into the life within the life of Christ's Church, since the main visions show the external aspects and the interposed ones the inner and more spiritual. The same division of four and three appears in both. The first four seals are introduced by the cry Come, the first four trumpets are followed by judgements on natural objects, the earth and the sea and the rivers and the lights of heaven, while the last three are woe trumpets announced by a threefold cry. The import differs, though. The seals answer the question whether the kingdom will now be restored, and answer it by showing that the way to rest is not easy; the trumpets are the voices of God's providences summoning the world to surrender.

Wesley states a rule about the whole book that this verse forces on him. The trumpets belong to the seventh seal as the vials to the seventh trumpet, and the parts must not be confounded; but it is not a certain rule that each part is fully accomplished before the next begins. Only the beginning of each part goes before the beginning of the following, so that the epistles begin before the seals, the seals before the trumpets, the trumpets before the vials — and what begins later may end sooner, or begin earlier and end later, the seventh trumpet beginning before the vials and extending beyond them all. He notes too that the place of the first four is specified in turn, east and west and south and north. On the instrument he is practical: when men wish to make a public matter known they give a token seen or heard far and wide, and none is more ancient than the trumpet, which Israel used in worship and in war alike. Robertson makes the connection backwards instead: these trumpets are soon to break the half hour of silence, and so grow out of the opening of the seventh seal, however that fact is to be construed.
3:
Who this other angel is has attracted more guesswork than the text will carry, and the four who address it disagree about whether it can be answered at all. Gill lists the candidates only to dismiss them — not a created angel such as Gabriel, and not any mere man, neither the pope whom Lyra proposed, nor Constantine, whom Brightman found here with the counsel of Nice, nor the emperor Theodosius praying before the battle with Eugenius. Barnes surveys the same field and declines to conclude, saying we have no means of determining who it was, and that all we know is that it was an angel. Wesley settles it by a rule drawn from the book: this is another created angel, as all of them here are, since in this part of the Revelation Christ is never called an angel but the Lamb. Ellicott refuses the question rather than answering it, holding that the designation another angel tells against identifying him with Christ, and that there is really no need to ask who the several angels are, the book being symbolical and the angels standing not for particular persons but for the agencies, personal or natural or supernatural, which are employed by him who sits on the throne.

Which altar he stands at is disputed, and Robertson is candid about the limits: the case endings differ between manuscripts, the word seems to mean the altar of incense, and it is not clear that apocalyptic writing preserves the distinction between the two altars at all. Ellicott takes the earlier altar in the book to answer to the altar of burnt sacrifice in the open court and this one to be the golden altar of incense; Wesley says flatly that it is the altar of burnt offerings. On what the angel is doing there the disagreement is sharper. Clarke has him about to perform a priest's office, and produces a detail from the day of expiation: on ordinary days fire was taken from the great altar in a silver censer, but on the day of expiation the high priest took it in a golden one, and while he offered the incense the people prayed outside in silence — which Clarke identifies with the half hour of silence in heaven. Wesley denies the premise. The text does not say he offered the incense but that he should give it; he discharged the office of an angel, not a priest; and the incense goes up with the prayers of the saints but not for them, since angels are fellow servants and not mediators.

Clarke reaches the same conclusion from the smoke: it is not said that the angel presents the prayers, only the incense, and the prayers ascend with it, the ascent being the token that both were accepted. Ellicott takes the mingled column as a sign that the prayers, no longer premature, are about to be answered, and draws the boldest claim in the pericope: these weak and imperfect prayers are invincible weapons, mightier than any carnal ones, so that as Jericho fell without Israel striking a blow, the Israel of God is omnipotent through faithful prayer, the judgements that follow being not asked for by the Church but the result of its asking. Barnes reads the same emblem more soberly, as meaning only that a church facing calamity would naturally give itself to prayer, which needs no historical verification since it is always so when danger threatens. Then the censer is emptied, and Barnes marks it as a new symbol and a reversal: coals are taken from the altar, no incense is laid on them, and they are flung down, as though prayer were now in vain. He finds the image in Ezekiel, where a man clothed in linen scatters coals from between the cherubim over the city, and warns against seeking a literal fulfilment of the thunders that follow.
6:
Barnes gathers the sequence before the first blast: the last seal is opened, heaven stands in suspense, the saints have offered their prayers, the censer of coals has been flung down as though judgement could be stayed by prayer no longer, and the angels raise their trumpets. Clarke says in a line what the instrument means — wars are indicated, the trumpet being the emblem of war. When the blast comes, everyone hears Egypt behind it, the plague of hail and fire that ran along the ground; Robertson calls the scene a semitropical thunderstorm and borrows Swete's phrase that the storm flung itself upon the earth. Ellicott presses the parallel further than the others and then turns it. The resemblance to the deliverance from Pharaoh is the hint of the meaning, reminding us that he who bade Joshua sound the trumpets at Jericho is the same God still; but the variation matters as much as the likeness, for this plague adds blood, and that addition carries the vision out of the possibility of literal interpretation altogether. He hears instead the figurative language of Joel about blood and fire and pillars of smoke, and recalls that Peter dated the fulfilment of that prophecy from Pentecost.

What the first trumpet was is where the room divides, and the division is about method rather than history. Barnes identifies it with the invasion of Alaric, working through the propriety of each element of the symbol and referring the reader to Gibbon for the extent of the devastation, allowing that a third part need not be exact so long as desolation spread over a considerable portion of the empire. Wesley looks east instead and finds the Jewish calamities under Trajan and Adrian, dating the trumpets from just after the Revelation was given: the insurrection of the year 114 in which he reckons four hundred and sixty thousand were destroyed about Cyrene and in Egypt and Cyprus, then the rising under the false messiah Barcochab, and the war to 135 in which fifty fortified cities and nine hundred and eighty-five towns were wholly destroyed. Clarke will have neither, and his refusal is the sharpest writing in the chapter. Some fruitful imaginations, he says, might find gunpowder and cannon balls and canister shot and bombs in the hail and fire; many eminent men suppose the barbarian irruption on the Roman empire is meant; but it is easy to find coincidences when fancy runs riot, and later writers might as well find here the Austrians and British and Prussians and Russians and Cossacks falling on the French empire.

Ellicott declines the same exercise on principle rather than by ridicule, reminding those who want limited historical fulfilments that the visions seem meant to show the general kind of event that marks the decay of the kingdom of wrong and the growth of the kingdom of Christ, such events being landing stages in an advancing progress rather than dated occurrences. On the wording, Clarke reports a substantial addition: before the clause about the trees, the Codex Alexandrinus and some thirty-five others, with the Syriac and Vulgate and much else, add that the third part of the land was burnt up — a reading he calls undoubtedly genuine and notes that Griesbach admitted it to the text. Clarke and Wesley then read the vegetation the same way, the trees standing for the chiefs of the nation and the grass for the common people, so that high and low alike were overwhelmed; Wesley adds that the Romans spared many of the former while the latter were almost all destroyed. Robertson keeps to what the Greek does, noting that the verb for burning up is repeated three times for dramatic effect, and pointing back to the earlier vision where the trees were to be spared and forward to the locusts who are forbidden to hurt the grass.
8:
Three of the four take the mountain for a kingdom, and all cite the same prophets for it: a mountain is a natural symbol of strength, being both defensible in itself and anciently a seat of power, and Jeremiah's destroying mountain and Daniel's stone that became a great mountain are produced in evidence. Wesley makes it a great force and multitude of people; Clarke adds that great disorders, especially when kingdoms are moved by hostile invasion, are figured by mountains cast into the sea, and that seas and collections of waters mean peoples, as this book itself shows. Barnes lingers on the picture before applying it, calling the mountain volcanic and reaching for the passage in Paradise Lost where the angels pluck the seated hills with all their load of rocks and waters and woods and bear them in their hands — though he grants the poet did not represent what John does. Robertson alone declines the whole allegory and reads the words as they stand: it is not a great mountain but a blazing mass as large as one, perhaps with the picture of a volcanic eruption behind it, such as Vesuvius in the year seventy-nine, or the eruption Strabo records which threw up a new island.

On what it stood for, Barnes continues the scheme he began at the first trumpet. If that was Alaric and the Goths, this is the next invasion to shake the empire, Genseric at the head of the Vandals; and since their power was maritime, the symbol of a burning mountain flung into the sea and the destruction of a third of the ships answers to it exactly. He then defends himself against the obvious charge with a remark worth recording, that he had worked through the interpretation of the symbol's language before he looked into Gibbon with any reference to the application. Wesley finds the barbarian irruptions too, but sets them earlier and takes them collectively, the Goths breaking in about the year two hundred and fifty and one nation after another following until the form of the Roman empire and all but the name was lost; the sea for him is the west, and Europe, and chiefly the vast empire in the middle of it. Clarke, having refused the identification at the first trumpet, refuses it again here in a single sentence: great commotions in kingdoms and among their inhabitants may be intended, but to whom, where, and when these happened, or are to happen, we do not know.

The fraction gets two treatments. Wesley denies that it need be arithmetical, since the words do not imply that exactly a third of the Romans was slain, only that an inconceivable deal of blood was shed. Clarke goes further and calls the third part a rabbinism for a considerable number, quoting the saying that when Rabbi Akiba prayed and wept and rent his garments and sat in the dust, the world was struck with a curse and the third part of the olives and the third of the wheat and the third of the barley was smitten. On the sea turning to blood both Clarke and Robertson hear the first Egyptian plague again, the Nile struck and the fish dying. Gill reads the creatures allegorically like the rest, taking the fish for men and the inhabitants of the empire, and noting that the Targum understands fish in one place as mighty princes and governors. Barnes keeps the maritime sense throughout and insists that nothing here is to be taken literally: the effect described is as if a third of all that was in the sea perished, and the ships destroyed are naval armaments or vessels of commerce, sunk either by contact with the burning mass or by the agitation of the waters.
10:
Barnes reads the falling star as a natural emblem of a prince or ruler, one distinguished by rank or talent, and takes the fall to picture a man who had left a higher station or whose course was like a meteor shot through the sky. He is careful about the kind of light: not a lurid or ghastly meteor but a bright and blazing one, emblem of fiery energy and rapid execution and splendour of appearance, such as would suit a chieftain of high endowments and impetuous character. Ellicott sees the same thing with one correction that matters, since the star is kindled rather than shining of itself — the light is borrowed, not inherent. He takes the blast to proclaim that the mighty who have been admired as luminaries, and perhaps worshipped, will fall; the rulers of earth, burning with lust of conquest or the pride of fanaticism, will be plucked from their seat among the stars. And he notes what the fall costs, since the fountains and rivers are smitten, and those are the sources of health and joy and the streams of prosperity.

Who the star was is the third round of the same argument, and this time one commentator names the others' answers and rejects them. Barnes continues his sequence and finds Attila, quoting Gibbon on how the empire of the Huns was divided among the sons of the dead monarch like a private inheritance and then extinguished by peoples out of the cold Siberian regions — which he thinks shows with what propriety Attila might be compared to a bright but brief meteor. Wesley looks to Africa, since it is a land of rivers and the Nile overflows Egypt yearly, and finds not a soldier but a heretic: Arius, a teacher of the church and one of the stars in Christ's right hand, who fell from on high into the most pernicious doctrines and made a gazing on all sides in his fall. He traces the consequences at length, the destruction wrought at Alexandria, the invitation of the Vandals into Africa in 428 through the intrigue of an Arian wife, the kingdom they held until 533, and his conclusion that Arianism was the inlet to all heresies and calamities. Clarke lists Attila and Genseric and Arius and one Eleazer who stirred the Zealots, and then disposes of the whole field: it certainly cannot mean all these, and probably none of them, and the reader may judge.

On the name itself Robertson is exact: the noun is absinthe, usually feminine but masculine here because the star is, and it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and not in the Greek Old Testament except in a later translator, though several varieties of the plant grow in Palestine. Ellicott supplies the scriptural background, where the bitter and nauseous plant stands for troubles and calamities — the people fed with wormwood and given water of gall to drink — and adds the warning against idolatry as a root bearing gall and wormwood, and the act of Moses grinding the golden calf to powder and making Israel drink it in the brook. He grants that some have taken the star for a false teacher whose influence poisoned the pure currents of the gospel and perverted men of original genius, that the passages he has cited favour it, and that it may be included; but he holds the main point to be the general stages marking the advance of Christianity, the fall of great men bringing misery after it. He ends where Wesley's reading cannot go, that all such false lights shall fall before the true Light and Morning Star, who will heal the embittered waters of life. Wesley for his part hears the title as exactly earned by the unparalleled bitterness of Arius and his followers, and notes carefully that many died though not a third part of them.
12:
The darkening sends everyone back to Egypt again, and Ellicott and Robertson both mark the difference as carefully as the likeness. There the darkness could be felt while Israel had light in their dwellings; here it is only partial, a third of the sun's light withdrawn by day and of the moon and stars by night, which Ellicott notes are far more needful in eastern lands than in ours, and Robertson calls a partial eclipse akin to the ninth plague. Ellicott hears in it the day of the Lord in which the light is neither clear nor dark, and the distress of nations with men's hearts failing them, and says such times must come, since the Church must go forward through seasons when the lights of human wisdom and of spiritual guidance seem alike obscured. Then he sets the trumpets against Genesis and produces the best idea in the chapter: read beside the story of creation these visions look like its undoing, the vegetation smitten, the earth and sea intermingled, the lights of heaven darkened, the living things in seas and streams destroyed. Chaos preceded creation, and through chaos again the Church must pass to the new heaven and new earth — the pulling down going before the building up.

Wesley reads the fourth trumpet as the extinction of the western empire and gives the calendar: after Theodosius died and the empire was divided, the Goths and Huns fell on Italy in 403 and 405, Rome was stormed and plundered in 410, Attila served the upper part of Italy the same way in 452, Genseric was invited from Africa in 455 and plundered Rome for a fortnight, Recimer plundered it again in 472, and in 476 Odoacer deposed the emperor and made an end of the empire. He supports the figure with a philological point that does real work: the Hebrews call an eclipse a stroke, and since such a darkness comes on not all at once but by degrees, so did the darkness that fell on the Roman world, the stroke beginning long before Odoacer. He adds that as earth and sea and rivers in the earlier trumpets meant the men who inhabit them, so sun and moon and stars mean the men who live under them. Gill offers two quite different candidates and settles on neither, that some refer it to the Eutychian heresy, which confounded the two natures of Christ and so darkened the doctrine of his person, and others to the darkness that preceded and introduced the papacy.

The last verse turns on a single word, and three of the four commentators think the familiar reading is wrong. Clarke reports that almost every manuscript and version of note reads eagle rather than angel, calls it undoubtedly genuine, and notes that Griesbach admitted it to the text; Ellicott says the best authority is against angel and translates a single eagle flying in mid-heaven. Gill lists the same witnesses — the Alexandrian copy, the Complutensian edition, the Vulgate, Syriac and Ethiopic — but shrugs at the consequence, since flying suits either and the sense is the same read which way you like. The other two disagree with him about that. Clarke makes the bird the point: the eagle was the symbol of the Romans and stood always on their ensigns, so that the three woes were probably to be executed by that people and upon the Jews, which he thinks makes the symbols consistent and appropriate. Ellicott dwells on its solitude and its height, a lone eagle crossing the meridian sky and therefore visible to the very horizon. Barnes, who keeps the angel, attends instead to the arrangement: the repetition of the cry is intensive, the three remaining trumpets are grouped as the first four were, and the interval between the groups implies that the earlier series had been completed before the later began.
